sections.title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

questions.q: What is a transition?
questions.answer: A process — a period of change from one situation to another.

questions.q: Name the two home-to-school transitions mentioned in the passage.
questions.answer: From home to preschool (usually around age three) and from preschool to primary school.

questions.q: How can a school reduce parents' stress during transition?
questions.answer: By supporting them, for example by giving them information in advance about expected changes.

questions.q: Name two challenges children may face when moving to primary school.
questions.answer: Any two: a sudden change to formal teaching, more emphasis on work, less time for play, fewer child-initiated activities.

questions.q: What do trusting relationships with familiar adults give children?
questions.answer: They give children security, comfort and a strong base from which to explore new environments and learn.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Children manage transition best when ________ provide support.
questions.answer: adults

sections.passage: A transition is a process which refers to a period of change from one situation to another. The home-to-school transition is the move young children make from home to a preschool, or from preschool to primary school. Transition from home to preschool normally occurs around age three. Parents can also find transition difficult, and school efforts to support them can reduce their stress and anxiety. Children who have attended an anganwadi, balwadi or preschool may still face challenges in primary school, such as a sudden change to more formal teaching, greater emphasis on work, less time for play and fewer chances for child-initiated activities. From infancy, children develop attachments to familiar adults; these trusting relationships give them security, comfort and a strong base to explore new environments and learn. Children manage transition best when adults provide support.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (match the columns, true/false, fill in the blanks or one-word answers).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (i) When children are about ________ years old, they are ready to go to pre-school. (ii) ________ refers to the academic knowledge, independence, communication and social skills children need to do well in school.
questions.answer: (i) three (ii) School readiness

questions.q: State True or False: (i) The transition to school is likely to be less challenging for children from financially disadvantaged families. (ii) Good transition practices focus on the whole child.
questions.answer: (i) False — it is more challenging for them. (ii) True.

questions.q: Match: (a) Reading readiness (b) Number readiness — (i) Visual discrimination (ii) Classification of objects (iii) Indoor and outdoor games
Match: (a) Writing readiness (b) Language development — (i) Storytelling and rhymes (ii) Drawing and joining dots (iii) Visual discrimination

Fill in the blanks: (i) Many schools offer children additional ________ activities before they start. (ii) School readiness recognises that schools also need to be ________ to meet the varied needs of children and families.
questions.answer: (i) orientation (ii) ready

questions.q: Answer in one sentence: (i) What is academic readiness? (ii) What is social readiness?
questions.answer: (i) Having basic knowledge of oneself, one's family and the world before entering school. (ii) Being able to get along with other children, follow directions, take turns and say goodbye to parents.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Differentiate between pre-primary readiness and school readiness.
questions.answer: Pre-primary readiness prepares a child for a preschool, which is less structured, like an extension of day care: basic knowledge, social skills, independence in self-help, communication and health. School readiness prepares a child for formal schooling with more complex activities for reading, writing and number work: following rules and routines, working alone, focusing and listening, and language, maths and general knowledge.

or.q: Describe any two factors important to successful transition in children.
or.answer: Any two: building on children's prior and current practices; giving children an active role in preparing for transitions with their families; helping them understand the routines and practices of the new setting; helping them negotiate changes in status or identity; and working collaboratively among parents, teachers and schools.

questions.q: What is meant by academic readiness?
questions.answer: Before entering preschool, children should have basic knowledge of themselves, their families and the world. Parents build it by reading daily, singing rhymes, showing the child's name in print, naming colours, giving puzzles and counting games and taking the child on outings.

questions.q: What do you mean by the term 'ready parents'?
questions.answer: Parents who understand the importance of early education and brain development, give a loving, nurturing home with age-appropriate toys, prepare the child for separation, make sure the child is toilet-trained and can express needs, and work with the centre for a smooth transition.

questions.q: What activities can a teacher do to promote writing readiness?
questions.answer: Activities for eye-hand coordination and small muscles: clay modelling, colouring within an enclosed space, drawing on a slate or the floor, tracing, copying forms, joining dots, drawing zig-zag and straight lines, tearing and pasting. Formal writing should come only when children are ready.

questions.q: What are the signs of a successful transition?
questions.answer: Children like school and look forward to it and show steady growth; parents are actively involved; classrooms create positive feelings; teachers, staff and families value one another; cultural diversity is celebrated; developmentally appropriate practice is visible.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Discuss the factors affecting transition to school.
questions.answer: The child's characteristics: temperament and personality decide how easily she adjusts; children with poor socio-emotional skills or low self-esteem, or without preschool experience, find it harder. Parents' characteristics: awareness, education and attitude to school. Community characteristics: accessibility and quality of local services. Transition is more challenging for financially disadvantaged, indigenous, culturally and linguistically diverse families and families of children with a disability. A sudden change to formal teaching with less play, and lack of support for families, add to the difficulty.

questions.q: How can children from financially disadvantaged families, children with a disability and culturally and linguistically diverse families experience challenges during the transition to school?
questions.answer: They are less likely to have attended an early childhood service, so they have had fewer chances to socialise and manage emotions. They may lack the competencies for a successful start, find the school's language, routines and formal teaching unfamiliar, and get little support at home; children with a disability may face barriers in the building and activities. This can lead to poor attendance and disengagement.

or.q: How can successful transitions from early learning environments be facilitated?
or.answer: By helping children understand the routines and practices of the new setting; building on their prior practices; giving them an active role with their families; helping them handle changes in identity; visits to meet the future teacher; orientation days; practising school skills; and a partnership between parents and educators.

questions.q: How can a smooth home-to-school transition be achieved in early childhood?
questions.answer: Through gradual change and familiarisation: visits to the centre to meet the teacher and see activities; showing the washrooms and lunch routine; reading books and telling stories about school with photos; practising school skills (opening lunch boxes, toileting, packing a bag, walking in a line, school songs); answering children's questions simply; giving parents information in advance; and building family-school, child-school, peer and community connections.

or.q: Why are trusting relationships with familiar adults important for children during transitions?
or.answer: From infancy children form attachments to familiar adults. These relationships give security, comfort and a strong base that lets them explore new places and learn. During transition they separate from familiar caregivers and must build secure relationships with new adults and children; the reassurance of trusted adults helps them adjust and manage their emotions.

questions.q: What is the role of ready families and communities in school readiness?
questions.answer: Mothers and family members are the child's first teachers: they give steady, supportive relationships and a safe, joyful environment, buy age-appropriate toys, prepare the child for separation and toilet training, and learn home activities that build readiness. Communities, businesses and government open quality day-care and ECE centres, provide space and equipment, educate parents about ECE and support anganwadi workers.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: What do you mean by ready children, ready parents, ready schools and ready teachers?
questions.answer: Ready children: the teacher observes whether each child shows demonstrating, approaching or emerging readiness and plans developmentally appropriate activities, materials and challenges; it is a continuous process. Ready parents, families and communities: parents give love, a nurturing home, age-appropriate toys, toilet training and help the child express needs; communities open quality centres and support workers and parents. Ready schools: involve parents and crèche workers; share preschool portfolios with the grade one teacher; have suitable infrastructure, a balanced, developmentally appropriate programme, child-friendly toilets, accessible shelves, a print-rich classroom with displays at eye level, enough materials and a good teacher-child ratio; respect individual differences; ideally the ECE centre is near the primary school. Ready teachers: understand quality programmes and child development, observe each child, give emotional security, keep a flexible, play-based approach, interact with primary teachers and keep upgrading their skills with the help of counsellors and special educators.

questions.q: Explain the components of readiness for preschool, with activities parents can do for each.
questions.answer: Academic readiness: basic knowledge of self, family and world — read daily, visit the library, sing rhymes, label the child's name, name colours, give puzzles and counting games, take the child to the zoo, park and post office. Social readiness: getting along, following directions, taking turns — set rules and routines, encourage play and sharing, model ways of expressing feelings, discourage hitting and biting, show affection. Independence: self-help tasks build pride and confidence — easy-to-fasten clothes, dressing self, simple chores, independent toileting and hand washing. Communication skills: listening and speaking are the first steps to reading and writing — regular conversation, answering questions, new words, songs and chants, modelling good language, writing notes. Health and physical well-being: balanced diet, rest, medical and dental care, immunisation, running and climbing for large muscles, crayons and scissors for small muscles.
